piece.title: String Quartet No.12 in F major, Op.96 (“American”)
piece.why: Pretty and clear, then a handoff: Violin I sings the theme, then the cello takes it over while Violin I drops to the repeated-note accompaniment on top.

roster.label: Church brass: 2 trumpets (one beginner), horn, euphonium

plan.summary: The tune starts in Violin 1 and moves down to the cello at bar 11. Here the lead trumpet plays the first half an octave lower. At bar 11 the horn takes the tune in the cello's own register, so the melody keeps the darker colour the composer gave it. The euphonium plays the bass at written pitch, so it really is at the bottom. The 16th-note broken-chord figure moves from the horn to the lead trumpet when the tune changes hands, so it always sits above the melody. The beginner trumpet plays the easy repeated-note figure in bars 1–10 and rests from bar 11, because there that figure would cross under the tune.

assignments.reason: The main tune (Violin 1). It goes up to A5, so it is played an octave lower (A3–A4) to fit the trumpet. The lead trumpet has the strongest singing tone. It stays above the bass now that the euphonium plays at written pitch.
At bar 11 Violin 2 takes over the 16th-note broken chords (about F4–D5). The lead trumpet plays them at written pitch, so the figure sits above the tune, as in the original. Keep it light and even.
Violin 2's repeated-note figure on C4–F4. It is easy and comfortable, so it suits the beginner. Ask for a light, detached sound so the tune comes through.
The viola's soft 16th-note broken chords (F3–D4). This lies well on horn, and the round tone blends between the bass and the trumpets.

At bar 11 the tune moves to the cello (A3–A4). The horn plays it at written pitch: a warm voice that keeps the cello's darker colour. It stays above the euphonium's bass and below the trumpet's broken chords.
The cello bass line at written pitch (A2–A3). The euphonium is now the lowest voice, under the tune and the broken chords.
The bass continues (C3–G2). Where the cello has a double-stop with a low C2, the euphonium plays the upper note, because C2 is below its range.
From bar 11 the viola has the bass (D3s, ending on C3) while the cello plays the tune. The euphonium follows it and stays at the bottom.

dropped.reason: Violin 1's repeated-note figure here would need to go an octave down for the beginner trumpet. That would put it under the horn's tune, and in bar 17 it goes above their range. The trumpet's broken chords and the euphonium's bass already give the same harmony, so the beginner rests.
